lesson.menu_title: Experience Counts — Twenty Years in Two Sentences
lesson.menu_desc: Saying what you have done, what has changed, and what you have not done yet -- 37 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 2 -- Experience Counts
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rosa M. Mitiko Shida | Lesson 2 -- Experience Counts

listenings.text: Rosa, hello, this is Carmen from the convention team. I am calling with two things. First, we have finally confirmed the dates. The regional convention is on the tenth and eleventh of November, in Bogota, and the invitations have already gone out to everybody in the commercial area. Second, and this is the part I need from you: we have asked every account manager to speak for five minutes about one client they have worked with for a long time. Not a presentation with slides. Just the story. Six people have accepted so far and I have not heard from you yet. Let me know by Friday, please.

Good afternoon. Before we open the floor, let me summarize what has changed since our last update in March. We have opened the regional office in Bogota and it has been running for two months now. We have launched two new routes inside South America, and a third one has been approved but not announced yet. On the commercial side, the four country teams have moved to a single reporting line, and nobody has lost an account in the process, which was the promise we made in March. What we have not solved yet is the reporting system. Three teams are still working in four different formats, and that is the first item on the list for the next quarter.

reading.rtitle: The Twenty Years Nobody Talks About
paras: Ask anyone in commercial aviation in South America how long they have been in the industry, and watch what happens. The number always surprises them. Twenty years. Twenty-five. People arrive in this business by accident, from tourism or from hotels, and then they never leave.

The industry has changed more in those twenty years than in the forty before them. Airlines have merged, disappeared and come back under other names. The corporate contract, which used to be signed on paper once a year, has moved online and is now renegotiated every quarter. Loyalty programs have become companies of their own. And the person who used to sell seats has become an account manager who talks about data.

What has not changed is the part nobody writes about. The best people in this industry are still the ones who have kept the same clients for a decade. They have not won them with a better price. They have won them by answering the phone on a Friday evening when a flight has been cancelled and three hundred passengers are stuck in an airport.

So when somebody asks you what you have done in twenty years, resist the list of job titles. The honest answer is shorter and much more interesting. You have kept people moving, and you have kept them coming back.
reading.source: Column -- South America Commercial Aviation Review

How much the industry has changed, and the one thing that has not
Why corporate contracts should go back to paper

items: Most people plan a career in commercial aviation from the start.
People arrive in this business by accident, from tourism or from hotels.
The corporate contract is renegotiated more often than it used to be.
It has moved online and is now renegotiated every quarter.
According to the column, the best professionals win clients with a lower price.
They have not won them with a better price.
The column suggests answering the question with a list of job titles.
Resist the list of job titles. The honest answer is shorter and much more interesting.

items.situation: At the convention dinner somebody asks: 'How long have you been in this industry?'
tips: Use for with a period, since with a starting point
Add one sentence about where you started

items.situation: Your manager asks whether the proposal is with the client already.
tips: Use already if it is done, not yet if it is not
I have already sent it / I have not sent it yet

items.situation: A colleague from Chile asks whether you have ever worked with an airline merger.
tips: Answer with ever or never, then give one detail
If the answer is no, say what you have done instead

items.situation: The regional director asks what your team has achieved this year.
tips: So far signals that the year is not over
Give one number and one name

items.situation: A client complains that nobody has replied to his email from Tuesday.
tips: Apologize, then say what has happened
I have just checked and the answer went to the wrong address

items.situation: Somebody asks what is still open on the regional project.
tips: Use not yet for what is missing
We have not agreed on the reporting format yet

extra_audio.text: Tom says he has read her name on the regional list and asks how long she has been with the company. Rosa answers with the number of years and mentions that she started in tourism. Tom asks whether she has already met the team in Bogota, and Rosa says she has not met them yet. Rosa asks Tom what has changed at headquarters since the announcement. Tom explains what they have launched so far and what they have not decided yet.
